entities.name: Inca Empire
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Inca Empire (Tawantinsuyu — 'The Four Regions'), the largest pre-Columbian empire in the Americas, extended at its peak (1438-1533 CE) from present-day Colombia through Ecuador, Peru, Bolivia, northwest Argentina, and central Chile — a territory of approximately 2 million square kilometers governed without writing, wheels, iron, or monetary currency. The Incas governed 10-12 million people through a sophisticated system of census quipus (knotted strings encoding statistical data), mit'a labor service, food storage, and 40,000 kilometers of stone roads.

The Inca expansion began under Pachacuti (1438-1471), who transformed the Cusco valley chiefdom into a continental empire in 33 years — the fastest imperial expansion in American history. Pachacuti's architects built Machu Picchu (c. 1450) — a royal estate and astronomical observatory on a cloud-forest ridge above the Urubamba River — that now represents Inca civilization to the world. The Inca road system (Qhapaq Ñan) — carved through Andean peaks and jungle, complete with suspension bridges, relay stations, and way-markers — was the most sophisticated infrastructure in pre-Columbian America.

Francisco Pizarro's conquest (1532-1533) was history's most asymmetric victory: 168 Spanish soldiers captured Inca Emperor Atahualpa at Cajamarca, killing 7,000 Inca warriors in a few hours. Atahualpa offered to fill his prison room with gold and twice over with silver — producing 24 tons of metal — before Pizarro executed him anyway. Within 40 years, disease (smallpox) killed 90% of the Andean population, the fastest demographic catastrophe in recorded history.
